worksheet.title: Fix the Turtle Code
worksheet.subtitle: Ontario Math C3.2 — find and fix code
worksheet.learning_goal: I can find the bug in turtle code and fix it.

parts.title: Find it, then fix it
text: Sometimes turtle code draws the wrong thing. A coder reads it, decides what it SHOULD draw, and finds the wrong number.
A turtle-loop bug is usually the wrong range number (too few/many sides) or the wrong turn. Help Bit fix them.

parts.title: Bit should draw a SQUARE — but this is buggy
parts.output: Only 3 sides — the square does not close.

parts.caption: range(3) leaves the square open — fix it to range(4).

parts.title: Find the bug
parts.prompt: Bit should draw a square, but the code says range(3). What range number fixes it? range(______)

parts.title: Fix the turn
parts.prompt: Bit should draw a TRIANGLE, but the code is:  for i in range(3): bit.forward(50); bit.right(90). The turn is wrong. What should right() be? (Hint: a triangle turns 120.)

parts.title: Fix the count
parts.prompt: Bit should draw a straight line 100 long, moving 20 each time. The code says range(3). What range number fixes it? range(______)

parts.title: Challenge
parts.prompt: Bit draws a square with range(4), forward(50). To make a BIGGER square, a student changed range(4) to range(8). That did NOT work. What should they change instead, and why?

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: To debug turtle code: say what it SHOULD draw, then check the range (how many sides) and the turn. Change the one that is wrong — to resize, change forward, not the range.

teacher_guide.eyebrow: Teacher Guide · Grade 3 · Intro Python Turtle
teacher_guide.title: Fix the Turtle Code
teacher_guide.subtitle: Quick facilitation notes & answer key

parts.title: Goal
parts.text: Students debug turtle loops (C3.2): decide what the code should draw, then find and fix the wrong range count or turn angle. The challenge separates resizing (change forward) from changing the number of sides (range).

parts.title: Curriculum (Ontario Math 2020, Strand C3)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential, concurrent, and repeating events.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential, concurrent, and repeating events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.

parts.title: Materials
parts.text: Python Turtle projected (or a web playground) to fix bugs live; the printed worksheet + a pencil per student.

parts.title: Run it (about 30 min)
text: 1. Run the buggy range(3) square; the open shape makes the bug visible.
2. Ask 'what should it draw?' then find the wrong number together; fix and re-run.
3. Students do Exercises 1–4 (Ex 4 is the stretch), solo or in pairs.
4. Share answers; land the big idea: range = sides, turn = corner, forward = size.

parts.title: Answer key (checked by the run-gate)
text: Ex 4 (challenge) — change forward to a bigger number (keep range(4)). range(8) just retraces the same square; forward sets the size.

parts.title: Watch for & differentiate
text: Common slip: changing the range to resize (Ex 4) instead of changing forward.
Support: write the GOAL (square / triangle / line) before hunting the bug.
Extend: ask the fix for a pentagon drawn with right(90) (use right(72)).

parts.title: Success looks like
parts.text: The student names what the code should draw, fixes the wrong range or turn (Ex 1–3), and explains that resizing means changing forward, not the range (Ex 4).
